extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, early chemists and dyers; readers of Philosophical Transactions
extracted.subtask_description: Experimental observations and practical inferences about how various salts and reagents change, reveal (latent), and fix colours in vegetable and animal materials for dyeing and ink-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acid salts advance colours of flowers and berries
rubrics_metrics.description: That acid salts advance the colours of flowers and berries; they make the infusions of balaustium or pomegranate flowers, red roses, clove-gilly flowers, mezerion, pease bloom, violets, cyanus flowers, of a fairer red; also the juices of the berries of ligustrum, of black cherries, buckthorn berries, of a much fairer red.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example reagents: oil of vitriol (acid) and other acid salts — used to deepen/redness in many flower and berry infusions; acid salts make little alteration on some white flowers (jessamin, snowdrops).

rubrics_metrics.name: Urinous salts and alkalies shift some flower colours to green
rubrics_metrics.description: That urinous salts and alkalies, on the contrary, quite alter and change the colours of the same flowers now named, and the juices of the same berries, also, from red to green; even jessamin and snow drops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alkaline/urinous reagents can convert red infusions into green; use with caution when preserving red tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urinous spirits and alkalies tend to preserve or advance colours of leaves, wood and root
rubrics_metrics.description: That in like manner urinous spirits and alkalies advance, at least do not quite spoil the colours of the juices of leaves of vegetables, of their wood and root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (from Mr. Boyle): urinous spirits/alkalies make yellow infusions of madder roots red; brazil wood purplish; lignum nephriticum blue; the red infusion of logwood purple; leaves of senna red.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acid salts change certain infusions from red or blue to yellow
rubrics_metrics.description: That, on the contrary, acid salts quite alter and change the said infusions from red or blue, to yellow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acids can convert some established red/blue infusions into yellow; implies complementary use of acids/alkalies to obtain target hues or to avoid destructive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red, blue, and white flowers with alkali become green then yellow
rubrics_metrics.description: That generally all red, blue and white flowers are immediately, on the affusion of an alkali, changed into a green colour, and then in a short time turned yellow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alkali (e.g., lye) causes an immediate green shift followed by yellowing—expect transient colours before final state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green parts strike yellow with alkali
rubrics_metrics.description: That all the parts of vegetables, which are green, will in like manner strike a yellow with an alkali.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying alkali to green plant matter tends to produce yellow dyes; useful if yellow is desired but destructive if green should be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yellow flowers are little affected by alkali or urinous spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: That what flowers are already yellow, are not much changed, if at all, by an alkali or urinous spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yellow pigments tend to be alkali-resistant compared with red/blue/white pigments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glastum sylvestre seed husks yield blue→green→purple (all fixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The blue seed husks of glastum sylvestre long gathered and dry, diluted with water, stain a blue which upon the affusion of lye strikes a green, which green or blue being touched with the oil of vitriol dyes a purple; all these three colours stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This material can yield multiple stable colours depending on reagents: water (blue), lye (green), oil of vitriol (purple). Example of versatile, fixable dye source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fungus tubulosus red knots yield purple with lye and stand
rubrics_metrics.description: On the tops of fungus tubulosus... are certain red knots; these upon the affusion of lye, will strike a purple, and stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain fungal pigments respond to alkali by shifting to stable purple—useful candidate for dye sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milky juices (lactuca etc.) reveal vivid crimson with lye but later yellow
rubrics_metrics.description: The milky juice of lactuca sylvestris costa spinosa, and sonchus asper et laevis, upon the affusion of lye, will strike a vivid flame colour or crimson, and after some time quite degenerate into a dirty yellow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some latent vegetable pigments give an initially vivid red with alkali but are unstable and later deteriorate to yellow—temporary colours may not be suitable for long-term dyeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milk of cataputia minor yields purple/blood red with lye then degrades
rubrics_metrics.description: The milk of cataputia minor, upon the affusion of lye, especially if it be drawn with a knife... will strike a purple or blood red colour, and by and by change into an ignoble yellow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handling and mechanical action (e.g., cutting) can affect the colour response; yields vivid but transient reds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hawthorn caterpillar produces purple/carnation with lye and stands
rubrics_metrics.description: The common hawthorn caterpillar will strike a purple or carnation with lye, and stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of an animal-derived latent dye that yields a stable purple/carnation on alkaline treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heads of beetles and pismires yield carnation with lye and stand
rubrics_metrics.description: The heads of beetles and pismires, &c. will with lye strike the same carnation colour, and stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain insect parts give stable carnation hues upon alkaline treatment—candidates for animal dyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amber-coloured scolopendra yields azure/amethystine with lye and stands
rubrics_metrics.description: The amber-coloured scolopendra will give with lye a most beautiful and pleasant azure or amethystine, and stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An animal source yielding blue/amethystine stable colours with alkali.

rubrics_metrics.name: No colour is truly fixed against all reagents
rubrics_metrics.description: That in all the instances above-mentioned, whether vegetable or animal, there is not one colour truly fixed; what seem to stand and be lye proof, are either wholly destroyed by a different salt, or changed into a much different colour; which must needs prove a stain and blemish, when it shall happen in the use of any of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that apparent stability against one reagent does not imply absolute fixation; test against a range of salts and fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both apparent and latent vegetable colours can be fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: That both the apparent and latent colours of vegetables are fixable: an instance whereof we may observe in the seed husks of glastum, and the use dyers make of the leaves after due preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper preparation and processing can render both visible and hidden pigments usable and stable for dyeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour of fruit/seed may indicate dye potential of the plant
rubrics_metrics.description: It is probable from the same instance, that we may learn from the colour of some part of the fruit or seed, what colour the leaves of any vegetable and the whole plant might be made to yield for our use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plant-part colour as heuristic when prospecting for dye sources; fruit/seed colours can predict leaf/plant dye outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent vegetable colours are pre-existent, not produced by reagent
rubrics_metrics.description: That the latent colours of vegetables are pre-existent, and not produced; from the same instance of woad, and likewise from this, that the milky juice of lactuca sylvestris affords itself a red serum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reagents reveal pre-existing pigments rather than create them; extraction/revelation techniques are key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour change in flowers is gradual and constant
rubrics_metrics.description: That the change of colours in flowers is gradual and constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect progressive and reproducible shifts rather than abrupt random changes; useful for timing and staging treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some flower colours destroyed by lye are irrecoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: That the colours of flowers, which will not stand with lye, seem to be wholly destroyed by it, and irrecoverable: Thus... one part of a violet leaf, upon the affusion of lye, is changed very soon into yellow, and will never be revived into a red by an acid salt; but if another part of the same leaf be still green, it will be revived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alkali-damage can be permanent for certain pigments; partial treatment outcomes may differ within the same specimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying may aid in fixing or preserving vegetable colours
rubrics_metrics.description: That the dryness seems to be a means, if not of fixing, yet bringing the vegetable colour into a condition of not wholly and suddenly perishing by the otherwise destroying alkali.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drying prepared plant material can increase resistance to alkali-induced destruction—consider drying as part of fixation protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials that yield multiple vivid, standing colours are best
rubrics_metrics.description: That those plants or animals that will strike different and yet vivid colours upon the affusion of different salts, and stand, as the cochineal and glastum, are probably of all others to be reckoned as the best materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer source materials that respond to varied reagents with several vivid, stable colours—these are most valuable to dyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: An exquisitely black colour resistant to fire and salt
rubrics_metrics.description: The author observes that he has found out a colour most exquisitely black, and comparable to the best ink, even for the pen, and which will not change by fire or salt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims a durable black ink/colour resistant to heat and salts; suggests possibility of producing long-lasting black pigments for writing and textile applications—would require replication and formulation details.
